parole.significato: -stan suffix to form country and province names, especially when added to names of traditionally Muslim ethnic groups.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Persian ـِسْتَانْ (-estân, “place of”). Doublet of стан (stan).
Borrowed from Persian آیتالله (âyatollâh), from Arabic آيَةُ اللّٰه (ʔāyatu llāh, “sign of God”), from آيَة (ʔāya, “sign”) + اللّٰه (allāh, “God”).
Ultimately from Persian بالاخانه (bâlâxâne, “upper room”), via a Turkic language. Doublet of балахана (balaxana).
Borrowed from Persian بهائی (bahâ'i).

It is considered a borrowing from a Turkic (Crimean Tatar, or rather Nogai) language paχn at, in which it is explained (according to Lokotsch and Miklosich, for example) as a compound word formed from Persian پهن (pahn, “wide, broad”) (cf. Ottoman Turkish پهن (pehn)) + at (“horse”) of Common Turkic
Ultimately from Persian پولاد (pulâd).
From Persian بوره (bure, “borax”).

parole.significato: guz (obsolete unit of length in Asia) (around two to three feet, depending on the region)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Persian گز (gaz, “cubit, a length of 24 finger-breadths, or six hands”), whence also Urdu گز (guz, “yard, three feet”), Armenian գազ (gaz), Northern Kurdish gez, Chagatai gez, kez.

parole.significato: Georgian, Kartvelian (person from the country of Georgia)
parole.testo: Modification of Old East Slavic гурзи pl (gurzi, “Georgians”). Compare also Old East Slavic гурзиискъ (gurziiskŭ, adjective), гурзꙑньскаꙗ землꙗ (gurzynĭskaja zemlja). Ultimately of the same origin as Persian گرج (gorj), as the word Georgia.
Borrowed from Persian گرزه (gorza).

Borrowed via a Turkic language from Persian جیران (jêrân), from Middle Mongol [script needed] (ǰērän, “antelope”), from Proto-Turkic *yẹgren (“yellow, chestnut”). Compare Azerbaijani ceyran (“gazelle”), Kyrgyz жейрен (jeyren, “goitered gazelle”), Turkish ceylan (“antelope, gazelle”), Uzbek jayron (“
Borrowed from Persian یلدا (yaldâ).

* Šanskij: зима́ (zimá, “winter”) + -о- (-o-) + род (rod, “born”) + -ок (-ok), literally meaning "born in winter". Parallel to Polish zimorodek. Borrowed from Persian زمرد (zomorrod) (per Burlak also the source of зиморо́док (zimoródok)). Doublet of смарагд (smaragd).
From Persian زیان (ziyân, “damage, injury”), influenced by изъя́ть (izʺjátʹ, “withdraw, remove”).
From Persian ایشان (išân, “they”).
Borrowed from Persian قلیان (qalyân).
Probably from Persian کاروان. Attested since the 1st quarter of 17th century.
Borrowed from Persian کاروانسرای (kârevânsarây).
From Persian مکار (makkâr), from Arabic مَكَّار (makkār), from the root م ك ر (m k r).
Via Persian مجاهد (mojâhed), from Arabic مُجَاهِد (mujāhid).

Derived from Persian نرد (nard, “backgammon”), likely through Georgian ნარდი (nardi) and Armenian նարդի (nardi). The game is most popular in Persian-influenced areas in the Caucasus and Central Asia. During the Soviet era it gained popularity in the rest of the USSR.
Via Turkic from Persian نخود (noxod).

Inherited from Old East Slavic обезьꙗ́на (obezĭjána), обозьꙗ́на (obozĭjána), further borrowed from Persian ابوزینه (abuzina), بوزینه (buzina, “simian”). Cognates include Old Ruthenian обезъꙗ́на (obezʺjána).
Borrowed from Persian پادشاه (pâdešâh).

parole.significato: hemp fibre (for making into cloth or rope)
parole.testo: Via Azerbaijani bəng + -ка́ (-ká), from Persian بنگ (bang, “hemp, haschich”).
Borrowed from Persian پلو (polow).
Borrowed from Persian شمشاد (šemšâd).

parole.significato: sarafan (a traditional long, trapeze-shaped Russian pinafore worn by women and girls)
parole.testo: Ultimately from Persian سراپا (sarâpâ, “from head to foot; honourable/honorable clothing”) via Turkic särapa(i) or Ancient Greek σάραπις (sárapis).
Borrowed from Persian تخته (taxte).
From Persian فرزین (farzin, “the queen in chess”).
Borrowed from Persian فیل (fil, “elephant”), from Arabic فِيل (fīl). Replaced слон (slon).

parole.significato: teahouse, teashop (a cafe that sells tea)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Persian چایخانه (čây-xâne).

parole.significato: attic, garret, loft (an attic or similar space)
parole.testo: Attested since 16th century. From Persian چارتاق (čârtâq, “four-arch”) via a Turkic language. Possibly a doublet of чертог (čertog). Compare Turkish çardak, Azerbaijani чардаг / çardaq, Karakalpak шердақ (šerdaq), шертек (šertek), Crimean Tatar çardak, Karaim čardak.

parole.significato: kaftan of blue cloth, with a standing collar and sleeves to the elbow (among some Caucasian peoples)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Persian چوخا (čôxâ), from Ottoman Turkish چوقه (çoha, “broadcloth”).

parole.significato: shawl (a square piece of cloth worn as a covering for the head, neck, and shoulders)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Persian شال (šâl).
